title: A JSON Block AST for Case Studies
description: I replaced my portfolio's hardcoded case-study data with a static JSON content system and a recursive block renderer, turning three flat strings-in-an-array entries into fully laid-out case-study pages.

sections.title: Case studies that couldn't say anything.

items.src: My case studies lived as flat objects in data.ts — a title, a description, and three strings called problem/approach/outcome. Every /work/[slug] page rendered the exact same placeholder regardless of what was behind the slug: a timeframe, a title, a description, and a line reading "the full write-up for this case study is coming soon." There was no way to show a decision, a hurdle, or a real metric — only prose paragraphs squeezed into a card.

src: Case-study content was three unstructured strings, unable to express decisions, hurdles, or stats as distinct, styled pieces.
Every /work/[slug] route rendered the same "coming soon" placeholder — there was no real detail page for any case study.
Case studies and lighter personal projects shared one WorkItem type and one card component, even though they needed different depth.

sections.title: A block AST, not a markdown file.

items.src: The content I needed — stat grids, tagged decision cards, chip lists — is block-structured, not prose. A markdown parser would have meant reverse-engineering that structure back out of text, so I modeled it directly: a small, fixed set of Block types (para, stat, simple-card, chip-list, and so on) composed through a recursive container, with every case study stored as static JSON at public/case-studies/<slug>.json and read at build time via a Node fs loader.

src.title: Full migration, no dual source
src.desc: The old caseStudies array in data.ts was deleted outright rather than kept as a fallback — JSON became the single source for case-study content, read by both the /work listing and the /work/[slug] detail page.

src.title: Section numbering derived, not stored
src.desc: The "01.", "02." sidebar labels are computed from each section's array index at render time instead of being written into the JSON, so reordering a case study's sections never requires renumbering data by hand.

items.src: Avoiding a heading-order bug baked into the reference design

The static HTML mockup I was translating into the schema marked its "hurdle" labels (e.g. "ENGINEERING HURDLE 01") as <h4>, appearing before the section's own <h3> — an accessibility bug, heading levels skipping out of order. Rather than replicate it, I introduced eyebrow as a non-heading label type in the Block union, so hurdle and strategy labels render styled but outside the heading hierarchy entirely. No block-level h4 was needed anywhere in the schema.
One route, two different content shapes

/work/[slug] has to serve both JSON-backed case studies and lighter projectData entries that still only get a "coming soon" placeholder. I resolved this with a discriminated union, WorkDetailResult ({ kind: "case-study" | "project" }), returned by getWorkItemBySlug so the page component branches on kind instead of probing for optional fields to guess which content type it received.

src.label: Lines of hardcoded case-study data removed from data.ts
Block types in the recursive content schema
Case studies migrated from flat strings to structured JSON

items.src: Model the content as it actually is, not as the medium you're used to.

It would have been faster to reach for markdown out of habit. But the moment I looked at what the content really was — stat grids, decision cards, tagged chip lists — it was clear a block AST fit the shape of the problem better than prose ever would, even if it meant more upfront schema design.
